finding.claim: Unauthenticated SSRF in /fetch2. The only check is a scheme allowlist (http/https), so an attacker can make the server request internal hosts such as 127.0.0.1, 10.x, or the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254. Redirects are followed because allow_redirects is left at its default. The first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller, so the SSRF is not blind.
finding.source: request.args.get('url') on GET /fetch2 (views.py:19), supplied by any remote client
finding.sink: requests.get(url, timeout=5) at views.py:22, with redirects followed

trace.note: url taken from the query string
is_http_url only checks urlparse(url).scheme in (http, https). It does no host or IP check.
requests.get is called on the unvalidated URL and the body is returned

finding.guards_checked: is_http_url is a scheme-only check with no host, IP or DNS validation. Redirects are not disabled. There is no authentication or egress filtering in the repository.

verdict.guard_found: none (only the scheme-only is_http_url at validators.py:7; no host/IP check, no auth, redirects followed)
verdict.reason: views.py:19 takes an attacker-controlled url, views.py:20 only applies the scheme-only is_http_url (validators.py:7), and views.py:22 calls requests.get with redirects enabled and returns the first 200 characters of the body, unlike /fetch (views.py:12-14) which uses is_safe_url and allow_redirects=False.

finding.claim: The /fetch SSRF guard can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (a time-of-check/time-of-use gap). is_safe_url resolves the hostname once and checks the resulting IPs. requests.get then resolves it again, so an attacker-controlled DNS server can return a public IP for the check and 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 for the fetch. This depends on the attacker controlling a DNS server with a very low TTL or alternating answers. Redirects are disabled, so redirect-based bypass is not possible here. The check also has gaps: it does not handle getaddrinfo raising an exception (this causes a 500 and is not a bypass), and its port argument is irrelevant to the resolution.
finding.source: request.args.get('url') on GET /fetch (views.py:11), using an attacker-controlled hostname and DNS
finding.sink: requests.get(url, timeout=5, allow_redirects=False) at views.py:14, which does its own DNS resolution

trace.note: url taken from the query string
private, loopback, link-local and reserved IPs are rejected
requests.get re-resolves the hostname, so the connection can go to a different IP than the one validated

finding.guards_checked: Checked the scheme allowlist, the hostname presence check, the IP range checks on all resolved addresses, and allow_redirects=False. These are sound for static DNS. The IP is not pinned between the check and the request, which is the weakness.

verdict.guard_found: is_safe_url (validators.py:10-18): scheme allowlist plus a one-time getaddrinfo IP range check. It does not pin the resolved IP. allow_redirects=False is set at views.py:14. No closing guard exists.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 takes url from the query string, validators.py:14 resolves the host once for the check, and views.py:14 calls requests.get, which resolves the host again with no IP pinning. A rebinding DNS server can therefore pass the check with a public IP and then serve 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 for the fetch.
